## OnnxRuntime.kt { #onnxruntime-kt }

ONNX models, running inside Field.

[ONNX Runtime](https://onnxruntime.ai) reaches the JVM through Microsoft's own JNI artifact —
`com.microsoft.onnxruntime:onnxruntime`, already on the classpath because
[`afield.ai.retrieval.SemanticRetrievalService`](machine-learning.md#semanticretrievalservice-kt-semanticretrievalservice) embeds text. [`OnnxRuntime`](machine-learning.md#onnxruntime-kt-onnxruntime) caches each session in a JVM singleton,
so re-running a box does not rebuild it.

Session construction is the expensive half of ONNX — hundreds of
milliseconds to several seconds, because the graph is parsed, fused and specialised for the
execution provider. Frame-time inference is the cheap half. A box that says `depthAnything()` and
gets re-evaluated on every keystroke must not pay session construction on every keystroke, and a
recurrent model (RVM, Silero) must not lose its hidden state either.

Field recompiles the *box*, not the application. The session map lives in an `object` loaded by the
application class loader, so the map outlives every recompilation of the code that reads it — the
same discipline [`afield.audio.synth.FaustEngine`](synthesis.md#faustengine-kt-faustengine) uses for compiled DSP. Key a session by something
stable (its [`OnnxRuntime.SessionSpec`](machine-learning.md#onnxruntime-kt--onnxruntime--sessionspec), i.e. file plus provider plus thread counts) and hot-reload becomes free.
Build an `OrtSession` yourself in box code and every keystroke costs a rebuild.

### Measured costs

Apple Silicon, 10 cores, Depth Anything V2 Small at 518x518. These numbers set the defaults:

 * **CoreML does not help this model.** The provider claims 43 of 848 nodes, across 19 partitions;
   the boundary crossings cost about what the accelerated nodes save (≈470ms vs ≈388ms for plain
   CPU — i.e. CoreML is *slower*). `OnnxRuntime.OnnxProvider.AUTO` therefore resolves to CPU. CoreML is still
   worth requesting for transformer encoders, where the partition count is small.
 * **fp16 weights are slower than fp32 on CPU**, ≈462ms vs ≈388ms, because every operator upcasts.
   fp16's win is download size (50MB vs 99MB), not speed. Pick it to save disk, not time.
 * **Pinning intra-op threads costs throughput.** `setIntraOpNumThreads(4)` measured ≈457ms against
   ≈388ms for the runtime's own default. `OnnxRuntime.SessionSpec.intraOpThreads` defaults to 0, meaning "let
   ORT decide". Set it only when you have measured that the render thread is actually starving.

The general shape: nothing on a CPU execution provider is frame-rate. 388ms is 2.6fps. Inference
belongs on its own thread with the renderer reading the most recent finished result — see
[`DepthAnythingWorker`](machine-learning.md#depthanythingworker-kt-depthanythingworker) — and resolution is a far bigger lever than any provider flag, because cost
is roughly quadratic in it.

### What is not here

The Java API (1.27.0) has no `IoBinding`. Outputs are therefore always copies, and zero-copy CUDA/Vulkan interop is not
reachable from Java today without dropping to Panama downcalls against the same loaded library.
That is fine for everything here: a 518x518 fp32 depth map is 1.07MB, and the copy is invisible
beside a 388ms inference.

Model download and caching is [`OnnxModel`](machine-learning.md#onnxruntime-kt-onnxmodel); [`DepthAnything`](machine-learning.md#depthanything-kt-depthanything) is a capability built on top.

## AI4FilestoreCli.kt { #ai4filestorecli-kt }

A command-line tool that uploads files to OpenAI through the content-hash cache and chats over them.

`main` reads `--file`, `--dir`, `--vfs-root` and `--vfs-file` targets (run it with `--help` for the
full list), uploads each through [`OpenAiFileStoreCache`](machine-learning.md#ai4-filestore-kt-openaifilestorecache) so unchanged content keeps its file ID, and
creates a vector store and file batch for the results when there are any. It then opens an interactive
chat thread through [`afield.ai.models.OpenAiIdeCodexBridge`](machine-learning.md#ai4-kt-openaiidecodexbridge), with file search when a vector store was
made and workspace symbol search when the Kotlin source index has definitions. The cache directory
defaults to [`FilestoreDir`](machine-learning.md#filestoredir-kt-filestoredir); the API key comes from `--api-key` or `OPENAI_API_KEY`.

## AI4_filestore.kt { #ai4-filestore-kt }

A local cache that maps file contents to OpenAI file IDs, so the same bytes are uploaded once per API key.

[`OpenAiFileStoreCache`](machine-learning.md#ai4-filestore-kt-openaifilestorecache) keys each record by a SHA-256 of the content and a peppered hash of the API key
(the key itself is never stored), keeps the database as JSON, and writes it atomically under a
read-write lock. `uploadIfNeeded` returns an existing file ID when the content is already known, and
[`DuplicatePolicy`](machine-learning.md#ai4-filestore-kt-duplicatepolicy) decides what a second upload of known content does. [`OpenAiFileUploader`](machine-learning.md#ai4-filestore-kt-openaifileuploader) is the
interface an upload goes through; [`OkHttpOpenAiFileUploader`](machine-learning.md#ai4-filestore-kt-okhttpopenaifileuploader) is a minimal multipart client for
`/v1/files`, and [`uploadVirtualFiles`](machine-learning.md#ai4-filestore-kt--uploadvirtualfiles) pushes Field virtual files through the same path.

[`OpenAiKnowledgeStore`](machine-learning.md#ai4-filestore-kt-openaiknowledgestore) is a second, registry-style store over the Files and Vector Stores REST endpoints.
The command-line driver for the cache is `AI4FilestoreCli.kt`.

## FilestoreDir.kt { #filestoredir-kt }

Where Field's derived completion indexes live, resolved in one place for every index that needs it.

[`KotlinSourceIndex`](workspace.md#kotlinsourceindex-kt-kotlinsourceindex), [`afield.ai.tools.GlslIncludeLibraryIndex`](machine-learning.md#glslincludelibraryindex-kt-glslincludelibraryindex) and the generated-completion-doc cache all read
their directory from [`FilestoreDir`](machine-learning.md#filestoredir-kt-filestoredir). The index is per checkout because `KotlinSourceIndex.runSync` indexes
`src/{jvmMain,personal,generatedLinalg}/kotlin` relative to `user.dir`: a single machine-wide directory
would let two checkouts, a docs build or a sibling worktree overwrite each other's index. Completion
ranking reads that index (a candidate's category comes from
[`KotlinSourceIndex.getCompletionCategoryForSymbol`](workspace.md#kotlinsourceindex-kt--kotlinsourceindex--getcompletioncategoryforsymbol)), so a shared directory would also make a test measure
whichever Field ran last rather than its own input.

Resolution order, highest first:

1. `-Dafield.filestore.dir=<path>`, which the build forwards to Gradle test workers along with the rest
   of the `afield.` namespace, so a test can pin a fixture index.
2. `AFIELD_FILESTORE_DIR=<path>`, the same for a shell or a CI job.
3. `<user.dir>/.field/filestore`, the per-checkout default.

On first use of (3) in a checkout that has none, the legacy `~/.afield/filestore` is copied in if it
exists. Those caches are expensive to rebuild: `filestore_cache.json` maps content hashes to OpenAI file
IDs, and discarding it re-uploads every source file. The copy happens once, is logged, and is
best-effort; a failure leaves an empty directory, which means a slow first run, not a wrong answer.
`FilestoreDirTest` exercises the default, the explicit pin and the empty-directory case. See `dev_docs/HERMETIC_COMPLETION_INPUTS.md`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/knowledge/FilestoreDir.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/knowledge/FilestoreDir/)

## deepsets.kt { #deepsets-kt }

A learned two-body interaction: the acceleration on a particle as a function of the neighbours
around it, fitted by autodiff from examples of any rule that can already be evaluated.

`flowMatch` learns `v(x, t)`: where a particle should go given only where it is. That can carry
a cloud onto a shape, and it is blind to the other particles. An interaction is the other kind
of rule:

    a_i = phi( v_i, SUM_j psi(x_j - x_i, v_j - v_i), MEAN_j psi(...) )

two small networks and a reduction over neighbours. This is the Deep Sets form, and its
aggregation is permutation-invariant over any number of neighbours, so one set of weights works
for a particle with three neighbours and a particle with three hundred. Classical boids is *one
particular choice* of `psi` and `phi`, so the family contains it.

### Why both a sum and a mean

Reynolds separation is a **sum**: being crowded by twenty neighbours pushes harder than being
crowded by two. Alignment and cohesion are **means**, since they are averages of neighbour
velocity and position. A mean-only aggregator cannot represent separation at any width, and a
sum-only one makes alignment scale with crowding, so `phi` is fed both, at a cost of
`messageWidth` extra inputs. [`DeepSetsWeights.sumScale`](machine-learning.md#deepsets-kt--deepsetsweights--sumscale) keeps the summed branch in a sane range.

### The feature map is where the physics goes

`psi` is not fed the raw offset. It is fed [`interactionFeatures`](machine-learning.md#deepsets-kt--interactionfeatures): the offset and velocity
difference, plus the **unit direction scaled by a small radial basis**, `u*p` and `u*p^2`, where
`p` is a bounded proximity that rises as neighbours get close.

Separation goes as `1/r` over a four-hundred-fold range of `r`, and a `tanh` network cannot
form the *product* of a direction and a steep radial profile out of Cartesian components at any
practical width. Alignment and cohesion are plain means, and linear in the inputs, so they
survive the raw encoding. Measured by ablation against the flocking rule: fed raw Cartesian
offsets the model reproduces those two to a relative error of **0.036** and separation only to
**0.78**, which is barely better than predicting the average.

A radial interaction is a direction times a profile, so handing the network `u` already
multiplied by a couple of profile terms states the *form* of a two-body law rather than
transcribing boids. The profile's coefficients, the velocity dependence, and how the summed and
meaned branches combine are all still learned.

### Trained by [`afield.math.autodiff.ADTape`](math.md#autodiff-kt-adtape), not by Smile

Smile's MLP cannot express this: the gradient has to flow back through a sum over a
*variable-length* neighbour set, and `psi` is applied once per neighbour with shared weights.
`autodiff.kt` is reverse-mode over a tape, which handles it without knowing anything about
networks, since the tape records whatever the forward pass did. Cost is one forward and one
backward sweep per batch whatever the neighbour counts are.

### The weights come out as [`MlpWeights`](machine-learning.md#neuralparticles-kt-mlpweights)

Both halves are packaged in the same flat layout the flow-matching work already uses, so
`MlpWeights.glsl` emits them for the GPU unchanged and the parity machinery in
`four.neural-field-parity.smoke` applies to them without modification.

## flowmatching.kt { #flowmatching-kt }

Flow matching over 2D and 3D point clouds — [`flowMatch`](machine-learning.md#flowmatching-kt--flowmatch) trains a velocity field that carries one
distribution onto another, and the field it returns can be sampled, integrated part-way, or drawn.

The idea is small enough to state completely. Pick a point `x0` from where you are starting and a
point `x1` from where you want to end up, and declare that the straight line between them is the
path a particle should take: at time `t` it is at `xt = (1-t)·x0 + t·x1`, travelling at `x1 - x0`.
Now fit a network `v(x, t)` to that velocity by least squares over many random `(x0, x1, t)`
triples. No two straight lines agree where they cross, so the fit cannot reproduce any single one
of them; what it converges to is the *average* velocity through each point at each time, and
integrating that average from `t = 0` to `t = 1` transports the whole starting distribution onto
the whole target one. That is the entire trick, and it is why there is no adversary, no sampler in
the training loop, and nothing to diverge — the loss is a plain regression MSE.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val target = flowSamples(myLine, 600, jitter = 4.0)   // sampled FLine + noise
val field = flowMatch(target, options = FlowMatchOptions(steps = 6000))
val cloud = field.sample(600)                         // fresh points from the same shape
val threads = field.paths(80)                         // the trajectories, as FLines
```

With a `from` cloud supplied it becomes a morph instead of a generator, and
[`FlowMatchField.transport`](machine-learning.md#flowmatching-kt--flowmatchfield--transport) runs the ODE only part-way: `transport(a, to = 0.5)` is a genuine
half-way shape rather than a vertex-wise average of two point lists.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val morph = flowMatch(to = flowSamples(lineB, 600), from = flowSamples(lineA, 600))
val halfway = morph.transport(flowSamples(lineA, 600), to = 0.5)
```

### Coordinates

Training happens in a normalised frame — the target cloud (both clouds, for a morph) is centred
and isotropically scaled to roughly unit variance — because a Gaussian source has to be
commensurate with the data for any of this to work, and FLine coordinates are usually in the
hundreds. The scaling is a single factor rather than per-axis, so it cannot squash a shape's aspect
ratio. [`FlowMatchField`](machine-learning.md#flowmatching-kt-flowmatchfield) converts at its boundary, so everything you pass in and get back is in the
coordinates you started with.

2D and 3D are distinguished by the data, not by a flag: a cloud whose `z` never varies is trained
as a 2D problem and its points come back on that same `z` plane. Pass [`FlowMatchOptions.dimension`](machine-learning.md#flowmatching-kt--flowmatchoptions--dimension)
to override. It matters — a 2D shape trained as 3D gets a Gaussian's worth of spread in `z` that
the field then has to learn to collapse.

### What this is not

- **Not a big model.** The default is two hidden layers of 64 `leaky` units trained by RMSProp,
  which is right for a few thousand points in two or three dimensions and nothing like enough for
  images. Training is single-threaded and per-sample (Smile's MLP has no batched matmul), so cost
  scales with `steps × batch`; see the timings in `FlowMatchingTest`.
- **Not able to change topology.** Integrating a velocity field is a continuous invertible map, so
  it cannot tear a loop open or join two strands into one — a flow can only deform. With
  `FlowCoupling.PAIRED` this stops being an abstraction and starts being the dominant error term:
  asking a straight segment to become a closed ring makes the mean landing error fifteen times
  worse than asking a small circle to do it, because the two ends of the segment are pulled to the
  same place and their paths have to cross. Give a closed target a closed source.
- **Not exact.** The field is an average over crossing paths, so samples land *near* the target
  distribution, not on it. Sharp corners smooth off, and thin structure needs more `steps` and more
  `hidden` before it resolves. [`FlowMatchField.loss`](machine-learning.md#flowmatching-kt--flowmatchfield--loss) is the training MSE, which measures the velocity
  fit and not the quality of the samples — judge those by looking, or with [`chamferDistance`](machine-learning.md#flowmatching-kt--chamferdistance).
- **Not ordered.** [`FlowMatchField.sample`](machine-learning.md#flowmatching-kt--flowmatchfield--sample) returns an unordered cloud. Recovering an FLine from it is a
  separate problem; [`FlowMatchField.transport`](machine-learning.md#flowmatching-kt--flowmatchfield--transport) sidesteps it by moving points you already have, which
  keeps whatever order they came in.
- **Not conditional.** There is no class label or text prompt input — one field carries one
  distribution onto one other.

## corpora.kt { #corpora-kt }

Synthetic drawings to teach a learned pen: Hershey plotter fonts and four drawing generators,
and a writer that turns a list of drawings into a corpus `python/fieldpen` can train on.

Every generator draws in the order a hand (or a plotter) would, which is the one thing a pen
needs from its training data and the one thing a scanned drawing cannot supply. [`PenCorpus`](machine-learning.md#corpora-kt-pencorpus)
resamples each drawing exactly the way [`Pen.feed`](machine-learning.md#pen-kt--pen--feed) reads a line, so a pen trained on a corpus sees
the same spacing when it is later shown a line. Tests: `PenCorporaTest`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/learning/pen/corpora.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/learning/pen/corpora/)

**Used in:** [Teaching a pen](../teaching_a_pen.md), [A pen that sees](../a_pen_that_sees.md)

Measured on the raw points instead, it mostly counts the small jitter between close points, and choosing by it picks the shakiest lines rather than the curliest. Marks of fewer than `shortest` resampled points are left out, so a line of dots does not count as curly either. |

Returns every cell with its correlation, strongest (positive or negative) first. |

Hatching scores high; a single wandering line scores near zero. |
| <a id="corpora-kt--joins"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">joins</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">line</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">FLine</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">within</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">4.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">recent</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">8</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">scale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">8.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">step</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.35</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/learning/pen/corpora/#L750) | How many of `line`'s strokes end on other ink: the share of its subpaths whose last point is within `within` drawing units of a point of any earlier subpath, or of this one more than `recent` points back. A web of cracks scores high; strokes that stop in mid-air score low. |

A pass is cut short where it would run into other ink, so hatching stops at the lines around it. |
| <a id="corpora-kt--pendrawings--twohands"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">twoHands</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">seed</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">words</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">6</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">hands</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MutableList</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="o">?</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">FLine</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/learning/pen/corpora/#L536) | A line in two hands: words that are either chains of small loops (hand 0) or sharp zigzags (hand 1), the hand changing every word or two. `hands` gets the hand of each word, one entry per subpath of the result, which is what a probe needs to find the cell that tracks it. |

## guide.kt { #guide-kt }

Guided sampling for a learned pen: the pen proposes several next points and a [`PenGuide`](machine-learning.md#guide-kt-penguide) picks
one. The pen keeps its hand (its tremor, its rhythm, its habits) while the guide decides where it
goes. [`FollowGuide`](machine-learning.md#guide-kt-followguide) keeps a pen a set distance from the ink beside it, which is hatching.
Tests: `PenHatchTest`.

## hatch.kt { #hatch-kt }

Hatching around a drawing with a sensing pen: every stroke of the drawing gets passes of the
pen's own trembling line laid beside it, which keep clear of the other strokes and of the
hatching already done.

A pen cannot remember which strokes it has not hatched yet, so [`Hatcher`](machine-learning.md#hatch-kt-hatcher) chooses: it hands the
pen one stroke at a time as a finished primer, with everything else on the page as
surroundings, and moves on when the pen has drawn enough or wandered off. Tests: `PenHatchTest`.

## pen.kt { #pen-kt }

A learned pen: a recurrent network that has watched people write and draws the next point.

[`PenModel`](machine-learning.md#pen-kt-penmodel) is a one-layer (or deeper) LSTM whose output is a mixture of 2D Gaussians for the next
pen displacement plus a probability that the pen lifts. `PenModel.distill` is the handwriting model
from Carter, Ha, Johnson and Olah, *Experiments in Handwriting with a Neural Network* (Distill,
2016), bundled with Field. `PenModel.load` reads a model retrained or fine-tuned with the optional
Python package `python/fieldpen` and exported with `fieldpen.export_for_field`.

The everyday call is [`continueWith`](machine-learning.md#pen-kt--continuewith): hand it an [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline) and get back the next few hundred points
the pen would have drawn. [`Pen`](machine-learning.md#pen-kt-pen) is the state underneath, for when you want to feed, step, fork
or edit the pen yourself. Tests: `PenModelTest`.

## penviz.kt { #penviz-kt }

Pictures of what a learned pen is thinking: its next-step distribution as ellipses, a stroke
coloured by one memory cell or drawn thick where the pen is sure to stay down, and the density
of hundreds of possible futures as an image.

Everything here reads a [`PenLine`](machine-learning.md#pen-kt-penline): its [`PenLine.history`](machine-learning.md#pen-kt--penline--history) for what it has drawn and
[`PenLine.distribution`](machine-learning.md#pen-kt--penline--distribution) for what it expects next. Tests: `PenVizTest`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/learning/pen/penviz.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/learning/pen/penviz/)

**Used in:** [A learned pen](../learned_pen.md), [Teaching a pen](../teaching_a_pen.md), [A pen that sees](../a_pen_that_sees.md)

## sense.kt { #sense-kt }

What a sensing pen sees of the ink around it: the Kotlin half of `python/fieldpen/sense.py`,
which has the canonical definition. `PenModelTest` holds the two together.

At each point the pen sees every point drawn before it except its own last `recent`, plus any
ink added from outside with [`addInk`](machine-learning.md#sense-kt--pensense--addink). Around the pen, `sectors` equal wedges of direction (sector
`k` covers `atan2(dy, dx)` in `[-pi + k * 2pi / sectors, -pi + (k + 1) * 2pi / sectors)`) each
report `1 - d / radius` for their nearest visible point within `radius`, or 0. Two more values
follow, the way to the middle of all the visible ink, `tanh((cx - x) / CENTRE_SCALE)` and the same
for y: what is close, then where the mass of the drawing is. Units are model units throughout.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/learning/pen/sense.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/learning/pen/sense/)

## Ai4Installer.kt { #ai4installer-kt }

Installs Field's AI assistant: the websocket handlers behind the box and document chat, and the code tools the model calls.

[`installAi4`](machine-learning.md#ai4installer-kt--installai4) registers the `ai-assist`, `ai-chat-*` and related message handlers, picks an
[`LlmBridge`](machine-learning.md#llmbridge-kt-llmbridge) for the configured provider, and keeps one conversation thread per chat key.
[`Ai4CodeToolProviders`](machine-learning.md#ai4installer-kt-ai4codetoolproviders) implements the tools that read, edit, compile and evaluate box code,
shared by the chat and the MCP backdoor. The top-level helpers ([`uniqueBoxOrRefuse`](machine-learning.md#ai4installer-kt--uniqueboxorrefuse),
[`setupSnapshot`](machine-learning.md#ai4installer-kt--setupsnapshot), [`clipToolText`](machine-learning.md#ai4installer-kt--cliptooltext), [`primitiveToolValue`](machine-learning.md#ai4installer-kt--primitivetoolvalue)) turn boxes and runtime values into
tool results.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/models/Ai4Installer.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/models/Ai4Installer/)

## AnthropicBridge.kt { #anthropicbridge-kt }

The Anthropic (Claude) implementation of [`LlmBridge`](machine-learning.md#llmbridge-kt-llmbridge), running Field's agent loop over the Messages API.

It uses the same `ToolRegistry` and tool definitions as [`OpenAiIdeCodexBridge`](machine-learning.md#openaiidecodexbridge-kt-openaiidecodexbridge). The Messages API
keeps no server-side conversation, so [`AnthropicBridge`](machine-learning.md#anthropicbridge-kt-anthropicbridge) holds each thread's history locally and
marks the system prompt and tool list for prompt caching.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/models/AnthropicBridge.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/models/AnthropicBridge/)

## AnthropicCredentials.kt { #anthropiccredentials-kt }

Credential + client construction for the Anthropic (Claude) provider.

Field's enterprise setup can't mint a raw `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, so the default
path here authenticates the way the official clients do: a short-lived OAuth
bearer token minted from an `ant auth login` profile via
`ant auth print-credentials --access-token`, sent as `Authorization: Bearer`
plus the `anthropic-beta: oauth-2025-04-20` header. A real API key
(`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`) or a pre-supplied bearer token (`ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`)
are honored first when present, so nothing here is `ant`-only.

This mirrors [`openAiClientFromFieldConfig`](machine-learning.md#openaicredentials-kt--openaiclientfromfieldconfig) / [`activeAiProviderRuntimeConfig`](machine-learning.md#openaicredentials-kt--activeaiproviderruntimeconfig)
for the OpenAI/OpenRouter providers; the client it returns exposes the same
`client.messages()` surface the [`AnthropicBridge`](machine-learning.md#anthropicbridge-kt-anthropicbridge) drives.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/models/AnthropicCredentials.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/models/AnthropicCredentials/)

## LlmBridge.kt { #llmbridge-kt }

The interface the IDE agent loop talks to, with one implementation per provider.

Both the OpenAI/OpenRouter engine ([`OpenAiIdeCodexBridge`](machine-learning.md#openaiidecodexbridge-kt-openaiidecodexbridge), via [`OpenAiLlmBridge`](machine-learning.md#llmbridge-kt-openaillmbridge))
and the Anthropic engine ([`AnthropicBridge`](machine-learning.md#anthropicbridge-kt-anthropicbridge)) implement this, so [`IdeChatHelpers`](machine-learning.md#idechathelpers-kt-idechathelpers)
and the installer can drive whichever provider is selected on /welcome without
caring which one is behind the interface.

The state/result types are the ones [`OpenAiIdeCodexBridge`](machine-learning.md#openaiidecodexbridge-kt-openaiidecodexbridge) already defines — they
carry no OpenAI-SDK types in their signatures, so they double as the neutral
currency here. The typealiases below give them provider-neutral names without moving
the declarations their callers already reference.

## LocalAiConnection.kt { #localaiconnection-kt }

The connection check behind the local-model panel on Field's welcome page.

Field asks the endpoint for its OpenAI-style model list at `/models`, from the server JVM, so no code
is sent and no inference runs. The answer says whether the endpoint replied, which model ids it lists,
and whether the one chosen in the panel is among them; a non-200 reply, or a body that is not a model
list, fails with that as the reason rather than as a missing model. A saved key is reused only for the
endpoint it was saved against, and a cloud credential is never offered to a local one.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/models/LocalAiConnection.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/models/LocalAiConnection/)

## LocalAiContextRecovery.kt { #localaicontextrecovery-kt }

Recovery from a local model that cannot fit the conversation: when a self-hosted, OpenAI-compatible
provider rejects a request for exceeding its context window, Field shortens the history and retries
rather than failing the turn.

`isLocalContextRecoveryFailure` recognises that case from the exception chain, including the empty
answer some servers return in place of an error, and returns false for a cancelled turn or a response
that was already partly delivered. `shortenLocalHistory` then drops older exchanges until the request
is about half its original size, measured in characters, while keeping the seeded start of the
conversation, the current prompt, and any tool call whose output is still pending; it adds a
developer-role note saying that older exchanges were omitted and that completed tool work has not been
replayed. Two rounds are allowed, and the failure after them is `LocalContextRecoveryExhausted`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/models/LocalAiContextRecovery.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/models/LocalAiContextRecovery/)

## OpenAiCredentials.kt { #openaicredentials-kt }

Where Field's AI features find their provider, API key, endpoint and model names.

Each setting is read from an environment variable first and then from a file under
`~/.afield/`: the provider (`AFIELD_AI_PROVIDER`, else `ai-provider.txt`, defaulting to
`openai`), the OpenAI key (`OPENAI_PLATFORM_KEY` or `OPENAI_API_KEY`, else
`openai-platform-key.txt`), the OpenRouter key and the per-provider model settings. The
/welcome page writes the files through [`saveAiSettings`](machine-learning.md#openaicredentials-kt--saveaisettings) and [`saveOpenAiPlatformKey`](machine-learning.md#openaicredentials-kt--saveopenaiplatformkey), and
[`aiProviderConfigRevision`](machine-learning.md#openaicredentials-kt--aiproviderconfigrevision) changes on each [`saveAiSettings`](machine-learning.md#openaicredentials-kt--saveaisettings) so cached clients know to rebuild.
[`activeAiProviderRuntimeConfig`](machine-learning.md#openaicredentials-kt--activeaiproviderruntimeconfig) resolves all of it into the one [`AiProviderRuntimeConfig`](machine-learning.md#openaicredentials-kt-aiproviderruntimeconfig) a
bridge is built from.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/models/OpenAiCredentials.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/models/OpenAiCredentials/)

## OpenAiIdeCodexBridge.kt { #openaiidecodexbridge-kt }

The OpenAI implementation of [`LlmBridge`](machine-learning.md#llmbridge-kt-llmbridge): Field's agent loop over the Responses API.

Each turn sends the conversation and the shared tool definitions, runs the function calls the
model returns through the `ToolRegistry`, and feeds the outputs back until the model answers in
text. Against OpenAI the history lives in a server-side conversation; against OpenRouter, which
has none, the bridge keeps it locally per thread. Rate-limit waits, suspended turns and the
request ledger are handled here too.

That response was made under "summarize ... without calling tools", and what the server keeps of it does not stay request-scoped, even with the stop sent as `instructions`. On house-machine-11 (2026-10-05) the forced final request also compacted the conversation (the next turn's input was 55k tokens, down from 100k); the next two turns, chained onto it, were offered every tool with tool_choice auto and answered "tool execution is still disabled here" without a call, though the first of them carried the reset note. 2026-10-04 had been the same, without the note. |

## ScriptedLlmBridge.kt { #scriptedllmbridge-kt }

An [`LlmBridge`](machine-learning.md#llmbridge-kt-llmbridge) that replays a fixed script of tool calls instead of asking a model.

Tests and the no-credentials mode of agent tasks use it to drive the real tool dispatch;
[`ScriptedLlmBridge`](machine-learning.md#scriptedllmbridge-kt-scriptedllmbridge) documents the script format.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/models/ScriptedLlmBridge.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/models/ScriptedLlmBridge/)

## StatelessHistory.kt { #statelesshistory-kt }

Keeping a stateless provider's conversation (local models, OpenRouter) inside its context window.

A stateless provider is sent its whole conversation on every request, so the conversation is ours to
size, and an item count does not size it: every turn's user message carries the full instructions, and
each of those copies stays in history. Three things keep it inside:

- `settle`, once per turn boundary: the finished turn's prompt is swapped for its durable text (the
  request without the instructions, which the newest message always carries), and older tool outputs and
  images are cut down. Done once, so the history stays a stable prefix for the server's prompt cache.
- `dropOldestTurns`, when an estimate says the next request will not fit: whole turns go from the front,
  always at a user message, so no function call loses its output.
- `contextOverflow` reads the window out of the server's own refusal, in llama.cpp's wording ("request
  (65833 tokens) exceeds the available context size (65536 tokens)") or vLLM's, which calibrates the
  estimate; the bridge then fits the request and retries.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/models/StatelessHistory.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/models/StatelessHistory/)

## VoiceTranscriber.kt { #voicetranscriber-kt }

Local speech-to-text for AI4 push-to-talk.

The browser records while the push-to-talk key is held and sends the clip as `ai-transcribe`;
this hands it to `python/fieldvoice/whisper_worker.py`, a Python process started on first use and
kept alive so the model loads once (`large-v3-turbo` on a GPU, `small.en` on a CPU). The worker
is an optional dependency (`uv sync --inexact --group voice`); without it the reply says how to
install it.

The interpreter is `FIELD_VOICE_PYTHON` if set, otherwise the one Field's Python boxes resolved
(the same venv the `voice` group is installed into), otherwise the checkout's `.venv`
(`Scripts\python.exe` on Windows).

One clip is transcribed at a time, on a dedicated thread: a second press queues behind the first.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/models/VoiceTranscriber.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/models/VoiceTranscriber/)

## MarkdownChunker.kt { #markdownchunker-kt }

Markdown cut into the pieces semantic search indexes and an embedder can read whole.

Four things go wrong when a page is cut on its `#` lines and indexed raw, and each has an answer here.
A `#` line inside a code fence is a comment rather than a heading, so headings count only outside
fences. The generated reference pages carry their `<span class=…>` markup into the indexed text, so
markup outside code is reduced to the text it wraps. A section longer than the window the embedder
reads (around 512 tokens, which `DEFAULT_MAX_CHARS` approximates) loses its end, so a long section is
split on paragraph boundaries. And a section alone says nothing about where it sits ("Kotlin side", of
what?), so every chunk carries a breadcrumb of page title, parent headings and its own.

## RelatedContextDiscovery.kt { #relatedcontextdiscovery-kt }

Suggests the guides and example files most related to a source path, for AI tools that hand an

`examples/` directory beneath `src`, `dev_docs`, `public` and `docs` in the checkout against the
path's directory and camel-case name tokens, and returns up to six of each, best first. The file list is walked once and each path's answer is
cached. An `afield://` path gets the connected compute-and-render example.

## RetrievalEval.kt { #retrievaleval-kt }

How well documentation search answers the questions the repository already asks of it.

Queries and answers come from two sources the authors wrote for readers rather than for a benchmark:
the text of every cross-link between authored docs pages (`[drawing with FLines](fline_examples.md)`
is a query whose answer is `fline_examples.md`; the standard anchor-text method), and the `why` text
of each `docs:` entry in the agent transcripts (`dev_docs/agents/transcripts/<name>.yaml`), each of
which says what a page explains. An anchor is left out when its text is generic (`here`, `this page`,
`api`) or points at three or more different pages; the page a link sits on is not counted against it,
since it contains the anchor text by construction.

## SemanticRetrievalService.kt { #semanticretrievalservice-kt }

Hybrid semantic search over Field's own source, the open workspace and the documentation, backed
by a local Lucene index and an ONNX embedding model.

Each indexed item is a [`SemanticCapsule`](machine-learning.md#semanticretrievalservice-kt-semanticcapsule) carrying an intent text, an implementation text and a
lexical text. [`SemanticRetrievalService.query`](machine-learning.md#semanticretrievalservice-kt--semanticretrievalservice--query) runs BM25 and symbol matches alongside vector
nearest-neighbour searches on the intent and implementation embeddings, fuses the ranks, and
filters by corpus (`field-internals`, `workspace`, `documentation`), path, kind, document, box
and property.

### Models and cache

[`OnnxSemanticEmbedder`](machine-learning.md#semanticretrievalservice-kt-onnxsemanticembedder) implements [`SemanticEmbedder`](machine-learning.md#semanticretrievalservice-kt-semanticembedder) with a Hugging Face tokenizer and ONNX
Runtime. The model presets download from Hugging Face through
[`SemanticRetrievalService.downloadPreset`](machine-learning.md#semanticretrievalservice-kt--semanticretrievalservice--downloadpreset); models, settings and the index live under
`~/.afield/semantic-search` unless `afield.semanticSearch.cacheRoot` (or
`AFIELD_SEMANTIC_SEARCH_CACHE_ROOT`) says otherwise.

### Rebuilding

[`SemanticRetrievalService.rebuild`](machine-learning.md#semanticretrievalservice-kt--semanticretrievalservice--rebuild) and [`SemanticRetrievalService.startRebuild`](machine-learning.md#semanticretrievalservice-kt--semanticretrievalservice--startrebuild) rebuild the index;
[`SemanticRetrievalService.startIdleRebuildWatcher`](machine-learning.md#semanticretrievalservice-kt--semanticretrievalservice--startidlerebuildwatcher) rebuilds when workspace documents change.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/retrieval/SemanticRetrievalService.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/retrieval/SemanticRetrievalService/)

## AgentExtensions.kt { #agentextensions-kt }

`agentExtension { }` lets a box extend its document's AI agent, beyond the single tool
`aiTool { }` gives it. An extension can register tools, context the agent should know before
every turn, a look at — or a veto over — every tool call, and slash commands in the chat.
Pi (earendil-works/pi) has extensions with this shape; what
Field adds is that they are live-coded. Every part is an ownership in the [`afield.runtime.lifecycle.LifecycleLedger`](workspace.md#lifecycleledger-kt-lifecycleledger), owned
by the run that registered it, so re-running the box replaces its whole extension at once, a run that
stops registering a part drops it, and deleting the box retires it.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
agentExtension("studio") {
    context("tempo") { "The piece is at ${bpm} bpm; keep edits in time." }
    beforeTool({ it == "DeleteBoxRequest" }) { refuse("Ask before deleting boxes in this document.") }
    afterTool { call, result -> if (!result.ok) println("${call.name} failed: ${result.summary}") }
    command("tempo", "show the tempo") { "**${bpm} bpm**" }
    tool("studio.bpm") { describe("The tempo."); action { bpm } }
}
```

### What the hooks may do

They run on the agent's thread, with a deadline ([`HOOK_DEADLINE_MS`](machine-learning.md#agentextensions-kt--hook-deadline-ms)); a hook that throws or overruns is
treated as "proceed" and reported, because a broken observer must not stop the agent. A `beforeTool`
hook sees the call's name, arguments, origin (the model, a tool program, the backdoor) and declared
effects, and answers `proceed()` or `refuse(message)` — the model then gets the message as the tool's
result. An `afterTool` hook sees a one-line summary and whether the call succeeded; it cannot change the
result. Context arrives in the instructions as document-authored data, framed as such, at most
[`CONTEXT_CHARS_EACH`](machine-learning.md#agentextensions-kt--context-chars-each) characters each and [`CONTEXT_CHARS_TOTAL`](machine-learning.md#agentextensions-kt--context-chars-total) in all.

Extensions are per document: they apply to AI conversations about that document only.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/tools/AgentExtensions.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/AgentExtensions/)

The file is deleted when `restore` returns, so read it there. |

### AiStateBlobs { #agentextensions-kt-aistateblobs }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">AiStateBlobs</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/AgentExtensions/#L419)

Branch-state snapshots ([`AgentExtensionBuilder.branchState`](machine-learning.md#agentextensions-kt--agentextensionbuilder--branchstate)), stored once per content: `<document>/ai4_blobs/state/` for a document that writes to disk, a per-process temporary folder otherwise.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <a id="agentextensions-kt--aistateblobs--put"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">put</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">file</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="n">java</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">io</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">File</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">box</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Box</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/AgentExtensions/#L438) | Keep `file`'s bytes, gzipped, under their content hash, and return the hash. The first put in a document each session also sweeps the states no conversation refers to ([`AiStatePruning.sweepOrphans`](machine-learning.md#aistatepruning-kt--aistatepruning--sweeporphans)). |

### BranchConflict { #agentextensions-kt-branchconflict }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">BranchConflict</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/AgentExtensions/#L479)

What [`AgentExtensionBuilder.branchState`](machine-learning.md#agentextensions-kt--agentextensionbuilder--branchstate) does when the state changed outside the conversation since it last saw it.

Constants: `KEEP`, `RESTORE`.

## AgentToolExtensions.kt { #agenttoolextensions-kt }

The registration point through which code outside the AI core, including a document's own boxes, adds tools to the AI4 agents.

[`AgentToolExtensions.register`](machine-learning.md#agenttoolextensions-kt--agenttoolextensions--register) takes a request class, an availability check and a handler;
registering the same tool name again in the same scope replaces the handler. A result type that
implements [`SummarisesForToolLog`](machine-learning.md#agenttoolextensions-kt-summarisesfortoollog) supplies its own one-line summary for the tool log.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/tools/AgentToolExtensions.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/AgentToolExtensions/)

## Ai4BackdoorTools.kt { #ai4backdoortools-kt }

The AI4 tool surface as an external agent sees it: the same registry the chat panel uses, wired
to one attached document, with every target named outright.

Building a context for a session assembles what a tool call will need: compiling and evaluating
Kotlin against a box, reading, writing and replaying operation macros, semantic retrieval over
the indexed corpora, text and symbol search across the workspace, the runtime providers for
shader reload and render-window capture, whatever tools the document's own boxes declare, and the
agent memory kept per document. The backdoor and the MCP bridge both call it, and so do the tests
that pin a tool's answer.

Targeting is the one place it differs from the chat panel. A chat tool may mean "the box whose
chat is open"; here a box is named by uid, by a name unique in the document, or by an `afield://`
reference, and there is no current-box fallback. A name matching two boxes is refused with the
count rather than resolved to either, because replaying a macro over the wrong box is the one
failure here that edits a document. A name matching nothing still falls through to the literal
uid, which is how a document root reaches its box and how a typo earns the provider's own
message. Passing a focus box names the box whose chat is to be played, which is how a backdoor
call reproduces what the panel would have answered.

Workspace text search is rooted at the attached document, the workspace and this checkout's
`src`, never at the process working directory, and refuses to run on Field's [`Runloop`](workspace.md#runloop-kt-runloop) because it
reads disk.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/tools/Ai4BackdoorTools.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/Ai4BackdoorTools/)

## Ai4RuntimeToolProviders.kt { #ai4runtimetoolproviders-kt }

The five AI4 tools that need the running Field rather than the saved document: reload a box's
shaders, capture the render window, list a box's Kotlin context variables, query the code-use
index, and search workspace symbols.

The in-Field chat panel and the backdoor registry share all five and differ only in what they
hand the constructor. The caller supplies how a box reference resolves and how to look a box up
by uid, which is what lets the panel mean "the box whose chat is open" where the backdoor insists
on an explicit target. The panel also supplies a staged-source hook, so a shader reload compiles
the text the editor is showing rather than the text last written to the box; the backdoor leaves
that argument out and compiles what the box holds.

Shader reload is the largest of the five, because one box can carry several shader programs at
once and a request may not say which to rebuild. An explicit mode wins outright. Failing that the
property being reloaded implies one: `vertex` and `fragment` mean graphics, `compute` means
compute, `task` and `mesh` mean mesh, and the ray-tracing stages mean ray. Failing that too, the
box is asked which programs it actually has and each is rebuilt, which is what `auto` and an
absent mode both come to.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/tools/Ai4RuntimeToolProviders.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/Ai4RuntimeToolProviders/)

## AttachmentExcerpt.kt { #attachmentexcerpt-kt }

Reading a long attachment one window at a time, under the guards every attachment shares.

The slice is taken after ordinary resolution, so an attachment already in the turn's context and one
the document's own resolver fetches are treated alike. The window is bounded (2 to 65536 characters)
and has to start inside the content. The content's SHA-256 comes back as `sourceHash`, and a later
read that passes it back is refused when the source has changed since, with a message asking for a
fresh read from the start rather than a splice of two versions. A `find` string moves the window to
the first match at or after the offset, with a little room before it, and an empty window with
`searchMatched` false says there was none. An offset that would split a surrogate pair is refused,
and a computed start or end that would is moved back one, so a window never ends mid-character.
`nextOffset` is null on the last one.

## BoxAiTools.kt { #boxaitools-kt }

A box contributes tools to its document's AI agents with `aiTool(name) { }`, an idempotent
Kotlin DSL that serves both the in-app chat and external MCP agents. A tool is a
`suspend` block that runs with the box in scope, can span many frames, and has its
arguments/description/return value marshaled automatically.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val a = aiTool("rectsl.run") {
    describe("Compile & run RectSL in this document's window, capture PNGs")
    val source by param<String>("RectSL program text")
    val times  by param<List<Double>>("capture times (s)", default = listOf(0.0, 1.0))
    action {                       // suspend; box in scope; may call frame()/delay()
        val d = afield.lang.rectsl.RectAnimationOracle.compile(source())
        if (!d.ok) return@action toolError(d.diagnostics)
        "compiled ${source().length} chars, would capture at ${times()}"
    }
}
// Test it yourself, same marshaling the agent uses — positional & type-coerced:
start { println(a("wall 1 1 ; rect 0 0 1 1 fill", listOf(0.0, 0.5))) }
```

The returned handle is directly `suspend`-invocable from box code — positional
(`a(src, times)`, coerced by declared param order) or named (`a.call("source" to src)`)
— so you can exercise a tool without going through an agent. See [`BoxTool`](machine-learning.md#boxaitools-kt-boxtool).

Registration is a side effect of running box code: re-running a box replaces its tools
by name (idempotent); a re-run that no longer registers one, or retiring the box, drops it —
see [`DocumentToolRegistry`](machine-learning.md#boxaitools-kt-documenttoolregistry) for the lifecycle.

### DocumentToolRegistry { #boxaitools-kt-documenttoolregistry }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">DocumentToolRegistry</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/BoxAiTools/#L486)

Document-scoped registry of box-authored tools. A tool registered by any box in a document is visible to every agent anchored in that document — the in-app AI4 chat and external MCP users alike. Keyed by document path; tools remember their owning box id so [`clearBox`](machine-learning.md#boxaitools-kt--documenttoolregistry--clearbox) can drop them on box disposal.

## DocsSearchBridge.kt { #docssearchbridge-kt }

The search engine behind the documentation panel, which retrieves from Field's local index and answers through the selected language model.

[`DocsSearchBridge`](machine-learning.md#docssearchbridge-kt-docssearchbridge) holds the conversation state and runs each query; retrieval stays local, and
only the synthesis step goes to the provider chosen on /welcome.

## DocsSearchInstaller.kt { #docssearchinstaller-kt }

The server side of the documentation search box: the `docs_search_input` Field message handler.

The prefix of `Message.uid` before `_` is the browser session key. One
[`DocsSearchBridge.SearchState`](machine-learning.md#docssearchbridge-kt--docssearchbridge--searchstate) is retained per key for the lifetime of this installer; there is no
eviction and no reset message, though every state is dropped when the AI provider settings change.
Work runs on the process-wide IO scope and replies are marshalled through [`inMain`](workspace.md#runloop-kt--inmain). Phase 1 is
provisional HTML and phase 20 is terminal HTML. The incoming phase is not consulted.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/tools/DocsSearchInstaller.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/DocsSearchInstaller/)

## DocumentGuideTools.kt { #documentguidetools-kt }

The AI4 tools for a document's Markdown guides: the durable notes and handoffs kept in the document's own
folder, its `docs/` or its `guides/`.

An agent can list, read, search, create, patch and append them. Writes are revision-checked: a patch or
append names the revision from its last read and fails on a conflict instead of overwriting another
writer, and create never overwrites. Mutations are refused on a read-only document.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/tools/DocumentGuideTools.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/DocumentGuideTools/)

## DocumentSourceTools.kt { #documentsourcetools-kt }

The AI4 tools that read and patch the live source of a box, navigate the editor to it, and export a snapshot of part of the graph.

[`DocumentSourceReadRequest`](machine-learning.md#documentsourcetools-kt-documentsourcereadrequest) reports the live, saved and last executed revisions of one property;
[`DocumentSourcePatchRequest`](machine-learning.md#documentsourcetools-kt-documentsourcepatchrequest) replaces it only when the revision still matches;
[`DocumentBoxNavigateRequest`](machine-learning.md#documentsourcetools-kt-documentboxnavigaterequest) opens the editor, box or output channel; and
[`DocumentSourceExportRequest`](machine-learning.md#documentsourcetools-kt-documentsourceexportrequest) writes a snapshot with provenance warnings. None of them launches
a box.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/tools/DocumentSourceTools.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/DocumentSourceTools/)

**Used in:** [AI4's built-in tools](../ai4_tools.md)

### DocumentSourceReadRequest { #documentsourcetools-kt-documentsourcereadrequest }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">DocumentSourceReadRequest</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">uid</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">property</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s">&quot;code&quot;</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/DocumentSourceTools/#L70)

Read one box property as it stands in memory, with the revisions of what is on disk and of what last ran beside it. Those three disagreeing is the ordinary state of a box being edited.

### DocumentSourcePatchRequest { #documentsourcetools-kt-documentsourcepatchrequest }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">DocumentSourcePatchRequest</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">uid</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">property</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">revision</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">contents</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/DocumentSourceTools/#L78)

Replace one box property, if its live revision is still the one the last read reported. A property that changed in between comes back with [`DocumentSourceResult.conflict`](machine-learning.md#documentsourcetools-kt--documentsourceresult--conflict) set and nothing written.

### DocumentBoxNavigateRequest { #documentsourcetools-kt-documentboxnavigaterequest }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">DocumentBoxNavigateRequest</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">uid</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">property</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s">&quot;code&quot;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">line</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="o">?</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">surface</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s">&quot;editor&quot;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">channel</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s">&quot;&quot;</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/DocumentSourceTools/#L86)

Bring a box, its source or one of its output channels into view in the person's own window. It waits five seconds for a frontend to confirm, and reports that the surface was opened rather than what is in it.

Write the live source and topology of some boxes, and any guides named with them, into a new directory as an installable snapshot. The directory has to be new, and has to sit outside the document being exported.

## GlslIncludeLibraryIndex.kt { #glslincludelibraryindex-kt }

[`GlslIncludeLibraryIndex`](machine-learning.md#glslincludelibraryindex-kt-glslincludelibraryindex) scans directories of GLSL include files, Lygia by default plus any roots
named in `AFIELD_GLSL_INCLUDE_DIRS` or repositories in `AFIELD_GLSL_INCLUDE_REPOS`, and records each
file's include path, content hash and declared functions and macros in `glsl_include_index.json`
under the AI filestore, so an agent can find which include defines a function.
`AFIELD_GLSL_INCLUDE_INDEX=off` disables it and `AFIELD_GLSL_INCLUDE_DEFAULTS=off` drops the Lygia
default.

## PresentationTools.kt { #presentationtools-kt }

The AI4 tools for a document's slides: read and revise an editable slide file, and inspect or drive a
presentation that box code has already built.

Those are two different decks. [`PresentationReadRequest`](machine-learning.md#presentationtools-kt-presentationreadrequest) and [`PresentationWriteSlideRequest`](machine-learning.md#presentationtools-kt-presentationwritesliderequest) work on a
`.slides.json` file in the document's folder, one Markdown slide at a time, and a write into an existing
file carries the revision from the read it was based on: a file that changed in between fails the write
instead of overwriting the other writer. [`PresentationInspectRequest`](machine-learning.md#presentationtools-kt-presentationinspectrequest) and [`PresentationControlRequest`](machine-learning.md#presentationtools-kt-presentationcontrolrequest) work on the
live slide show of a box that built a presentation in Kotlin — inspect reports its steps, current cue and
checkpoint, control navigates it. Control can run a step's own callbacks, so what it reports is the state
of the JVM rather than proof that an audience saw anything.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/tools/PresentationTools.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/PresentationTools/)

## RepoFileTools.kt { #repofiletools-kt }

The `repo` tools read, list, search, patch and create files in one checkout, for a job that hands
AI4 work a coding agent would otherwise do (a docs-notes revision, a landing question). A job
supplies a [`RepoScope`](machine-learning.md#repofiletools-kt-reposcope): the root, the globs it may read and the globs it may write. Every path is
relative to the root with `/` separators; an absolute path, a `..` segment, a symbolic link
anywhere on the way, `.git`, or a path no glob admits is refused with the reason. The tools are
offered only when a job wires a scope ([`ToolExecutionContext.repoFiles`](machine-learning.md#tools-kt--toolexecutioncontext--repofiles)); a chat never sees them.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/tools/RepoFileTools.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/RepoFileTools/)

## StateTools.kt { #statetools-kt }

The AI4 tools that list, read, show and fork the saved histories of a document, over the same providers the States browser shows a person.

[`StateListRequest`](machine-learning.md#statetools-kt-statelistrequest), [`StateReadRequest`](machine-learning.md#statetools-kt-statereadrequest), [`StateShowRequest`](machine-learning.md#statetools-kt-stateshowrequest) and [`StateForkRequest`](machine-learning.md#statetools-kt-stateforkrequest) are the tools,
and [`StateToolResult`](machine-learning.md#statetools-kt-statetoolresult) is their answer. None of them restores a state or runs code; forking is
offered only by a history that reports `canFork`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/tools/StateTools.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/StateTools/)

**Used in:** [AI4's built-in tools](../ai4_tools.md)

### StateListRequest { #statetools-kt-statelistrequest }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">StateListRequest</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">history</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s">&quot;&quot;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">query</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s">&quot;&quot;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">offset</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">limit</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">40</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/StateTools/#L63)

List the histories, or the saved states inside one of them. With `history` empty the answer's [`StateToolResult.histories`](machine-learning.md#statetools-kt--statetoolresult--histories) names every history this document has; with it set, [`StateToolResult.nodes`](machine-learning.md#statetools-kt--statetoolresult--nodes) is a page of that history's states.

### StateReadRequest { #statetools-kt-statereadrequest }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">StateReadRequest</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">history</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">state</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">startChar</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">maxChars</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">6000</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">revision</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s">&quot;&quot;</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/StateTools/#L72)

Read one saved state's text, a page at a time. The whole text is hashed into [`StateToolResult.revision`](machine-learning.md#statetools-kt--statetoolresult--revision); passing that revision back on a later page makes a provider whose data changed mid-read fail rather than stitch two versions together.

### StateShowRequest { #statetools-kt-stateshowrequest }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">StateShowRequest</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">history</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">state</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s">&quot;&quot;</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/StateTools/#L80)

Reveal a history, and optionally one of its states, in the person's own state browser. This is the one tool here that needs a connected frontend: with none, it answers unsuccessfully within twenty seconds.

### StateForkRequest { #statetools-kt-stateforkrequest }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">StateForkRequest</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">history</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">state</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/StateTools/#L88)

Branch from a saved state under a new name, leaving the active state where it is. Only a history whose provider supplies a fork can do this, which is what [`StateHistoryInfo`](machine-learning.md#statetools-kt-statehistoryinfo) reports as `canFork`.

### StateHistoryInfo { #statetools-kt-statehistoryinfo }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">StateHistoryInfo</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">id</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">canFork</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/StateTools/#L91)

One history in a listing: its exact `id`, the label the browser shows, and whether it can fork.

## StateTreeBrowser.kt { #statetreebrowser-kt }

The States browser of AI4: how a box exposes a saved history with [`stateTree`](machine-learning.md#statetreebrowser-kt--statetree), and the read-only view of it shared by the browser and by chat references.

A provider supplies a snapshot, a reader for one saved state and, optionally, a fork callback.
[`StateTreeBrowser`](machine-learning.md#statetreebrowser-kt-statetreebrowser) pages and bounds the text it shows, and never restores a state.

## ToolMeta.kt { #toolmeta-kt }

Tool metadata answers three questions beyond the schema: which namespace a tool belongs to, how the
model discovers it ([`ToolExposure`](machine-learning.md#toolmeta-kt-toolexposure)), and what calling it does ([`ToolEffect`](machine-learning.md#toolmeta-kt-tooleffect)). Both of the last two
follow Pi (earendil-works/pi). Exposure decides whether a tool's schema is sent with every request or
only on demand. Field uses effects for three things rather than for confirmation dialogs: a central
refusal of document mutations on a read-only document, eval checks
(`effects-absent:FILESYSTEM_WRITE`), and the catalogue line that tells a model which calls are cheap
looks and which change things.

Metadata comes from [`AgentToolMeta`](machine-learning.md#toolmeta-kt-agenttoolmeta) on the request class, from `aiTool { namespace(); exposure();
effects() }` for a box-authored tool, or from `AgentToolExtensions.register(meta = ...)`. A class with
none gets `ToolMeta.DEFAULT`: namespace `core`, DIRECT, `ToolEffect.UNDECLARED` — undeclared rather
than "no effects", so an eval asserting an effect is absent fails on a tool that never said.

## ToolRunloopDispatch.kt { #toolrunloopdispatch-kt }

The check that turns a deadlocking `aiTool` call into an error message.

A tool body runs on the Runloop's main thread, so a caller that is already blocking that thread inside
`runBlocking` can never let the body run: the call would wait for a thread that is waiting for it.
Giving the `runBlocking` a `Dispatchers.IO` context moves the body but not the blocked caller, so that
case is checked as well, by looking for `runBlocking` on the owning thread's stack. Both messages name
the two ways of calling a tool that do work: directly from AI4, or inside `start { ... }` in box code.

## Tools.kt { #tools-kt }

The request and result classes of the tools Field's AI agent can call, and the registry that
dispatches a call by name to its handler.

Each tool is a Kotlin data class: its simple name is the tool name, `@JsonClassDescription` and
`@JsonPropertyDescription` are what the model reads, and [`AgentToolMeta`](machine-learning.md#toolmeta-kt-agenttoolmeta) records the tool's group
and effects. The file covers attachments and definitions, Kotlin compile and evaluate, shader
reload, render-window capture, macros, code-use queries, and the agent's scratchpad and checklist
([`AgentMemoryState`](machine-learning.md#tools-kt-agentmemorystate)). A result that carries pictures implements [`CarriesToolImages`](machine-learning.md#tools-kt-carriestoolimages), so the images
travel as images rather than as base64 text inside the JSON output.

`ToolSchema` emits the JSON Schema for a request class from Kotlin reflection alone, skipping
`@JsonIgnore` and placeholder `unused` fields; `openAiTool` builds the OpenAI function tool and
keeps nullable arguments optional. `AgentToolSchemaTest` checks that OpenAI accepts the argument
schema of every registered tool.

## TutorialCodeTools.kt { #tutorialcodetools-kt }

Finding tutorial code: a worked example of box code to start from.

Field ships about 260 tutorial documents: the materialized agent transcripts under
`public/docs/assets/agent_transcripts/<name>/` and the graphics curriculum in
`public/docs/assets/canonical_graphics/`. Semantic search indexes them box by box as its `tutorials` corpus,
the way it indexes a workspace; this tool is a query on that corpus, grouped by document (by lesson for the
graphics curriculum, whose boxes are its lessons), with each document's description and docs links from its
transcript and the code files to read. A match names files rather than quoting them: read one with
[`AttachmentRequest`](machine-learning.md#tools-kt-attachmentrequest) to see the box code itself.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/tools/TutorialCodeTools.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/TutorialCodeTools/)

## WorkspaceSearch.kt { #workspacesearch-kt }

`WorkspaceSearchRequest` is the agent tool that finds literal text in exactly one
[`WorkspaceSearchScope`](machine-learning.md#workspacesearch-kt-workspacesearchscope): the current document's files, its history, the whole workspace, or Field's
own Kotlin source. It reads one bounded file at a time under byte, match and time limits, and the
[`WorkspaceSearchResult`](machine-learning.md#workspacesearch-kt-workspacesearchresult) says whether it is complete and, if not, why it stopped and what it skipped.
There is no regex or shell syntax, and unsaved editor state is not searched.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/tools/WorkspaceSearch.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/WorkspaceSearch/)

## ToolEvidence.kt { #toolevidence-kt }

Complete tool results that are too large for a transcript, kept whole outside the model's context.

A program's nested calls are recorded in the turn's transcript and the tool I/O log, but a result of
tens of kilobytes would make both unreadable, and cutting it at a fixed length leaves invalid JSON
that hides exactly the part of a failure the next agent needs. So a nested result over
`ToolProgramRunner.MAX_NESTED_RESULT_CHARS` is stored here whole, content-addressed, and the transcript
carries a small, valid stub with its id, SHA-256 and size; [`ReadToolEvidenceRequest`](machine-learning.md#toolevidence-kt-readtoolevidencerequest) reads it back.

[`store`](machine-learning.md#toolevidence-kt--toolevidence--store-2) is replaceable: a host with its own evidence store (a study's build records, say) can put
these there instead. The default keeps them gzipped beside the tool I/O log,
`~/.afield/logs/ai4_tool_io/evidence/` (`AFIELD_AI4_TOOL_EVIDENCE_PATH` or
`-Dafield.ai4.toolEvidence.path` to move it). Nothing deletes them yet.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/tools/program/ToolEvidence.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/program/ToolEvidence/)

## ToolProgramRunner.kt { #toolprogramrunner-kt }

The sandbox a tool program runs in: one [`RunToolProgramRequest`](machine-learning.md#toolprogramtools-kt-runtoolprogramrequest)'s JavaScript, in a fresh GraalJS
context that can reach the conversation's tools and nothing else. [`RunToolProgramRequest`](machine-learning.md#toolprogramtools-kt-runtoolprogramrequest)'s own
file overview says what a program is for; this file is how it is kept to its tools.

### The boundary

Only strings cross it. The guest gets six host functions (`__call`, `__out`, `__progress`, `__show`,
`__describe`, `__settle`) and one JSON string of tool names; a prelude builds the friendly
`tools.X(...)`, `tools.X.raw(...)`, `check(...)`, `progress(...)`, `text(...)` and `show(...)` surface from
those in JS. The context runs under `SandboxPolicy.CONSTRAINED` with no IO, no threads, no processes,
no native access, no polyglot access, no environment and no host class lookup, and carries a statement
limit, so a program cannot reach a Java object even by accident.

### Ending a program

A program ends by settling its promise (stage `ok`; or `tool-failed` for an uncaught failing call,
`check-failed` for an uncaught `check`, `runtime` for any other error), by a syntax error, by running out
of statements, calls or time, or because its turn was cancelled. Time and cancellation are a watchdog's job:
it closes the context from its own thread, which Graal honours the next time the program thread is in
guest code, so a tool call already running is allowed to finish. A cancellation is rethrown as a
`CancellationException` so the turn ends rather than reporting a tool error, matching every bridge's
`isAiTurnCancellation` handling.

### Threads

The program runs on the calling thread, which is the agent loop's: an IO thread for a panel turn, a
daemon for an agent task, the backdoor's scope for MCP. Never the Runloop — the graph tools a program
calls hop onto the Runloop and wait for it, which would deadlock there, so `run` refuses.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/tools/program/ToolProgramRunner.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/program/ToolProgramRunner/)

## ToolProgramTools.kt { #toolprogramtools-kt }

[`RunToolProgramRequest`](machine-learning.md#toolprogramtools-kt-runtoolprogramrequest) is one tool whose argument is a short JavaScript program, so a model that
would have spent twelve rounds calling twelve tools spends one. The program can
call every other tool the conversation has, as a function — `tools.RunBox({box: "Cell03"})` — and
only what it returns, or prints with `text(...)`, goes back to the model, plus a one-line record per
call. The intermediate results stay in the program. The idea is Pi's "codemode"
(earendil-works/pi); the mapping onto Field is in `dev_docs/ai/AI4_PI_LESSONS.md`.

The saving is in what a round costs. A model working through tools one call per round pays for
every round twice: a request carrying the whole conversation so far, and a result that lands in
that conversation for good. For "run each of these twelve boxes and tell me which ones fail" that
is twelve rounds and twelve results the model reads in full, when what it needed was three names.

### What a program can reach

Only the tools, and only through one string-in, string-out bridge: the runner builds a
GraalJS context with no host access, no IO, no threads, no processes, no environment and a
statement limit, so there is no `Java.type`, no `require`, no `fetch` and no timers. A tool call
from a program goes through `ToolRegistry.executeByName` — the same dispatcher a model's own call
goes through, with the same gates — so a program can do nothing the conversation could not do one
call at a time, and every edit it makes is recorded exactly as the direct call would record it.

A program is not a transaction. One that fails halfway leaves its earlier edits in place; they are
recorded and undoable like any other agent edit, but nothing rolls them back.

### Why JavaScript and not the macro YAML

What makes this pay is the middle of the program — filter, loop, branch on a result — and the
OperationTranscript YAML has no data flow at all: it is the durable, reversible record of
edits, and the edits a program makes still land there. Kotlin would be the house language, but every
program would pay a K2 compile, and box code can reach the whole JVM. JS is what models write
fluently as glue, and GraalJS is already on the classpath.

## AiToolUseImprovementCli.kt { #aitooluseimprovementcli-kt }

A command-line task in which a model reads Field's recent AI tool I/O logs and edits the AI4 tool
descriptions and prompts that caused the trouble it finds.

[`main`](machine-learning.md#aitooluseimprovementcli-kt--main) runs it; Gradle's `improveAiToolUse` and `improveAiToolUseDryRun` tasks launch it. It
summarises the newest logs under `~/.afield/logs/ai4_tool_io/` (`--log-dir`, or
`AFIELD_AI4_TOOL_IO_LOG_PATH`), attaches a manifest of the source tree, and gives the model a small
tool set over it, including `ReplaceInFileRequest` for exact snippet edits. It writes a Markdown
report and a transcript of the run. With `--dry-run` the edits go to an in-memory overlay and come
out as a patch file instead of touching the source. Logs of this task's own runs are left out of the
review ([`isToolUseImprovementLog`](machine-learning.md#aitooluseimprovementcli-kt--istooluseimprovementlog)).

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/tools/tooluse/AiToolUseImprovementCli.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/tooluse/AiToolUseImprovementCli/)

## stippletransport.kt { #stippletransport-kt }

Runs a learned stipple transport on the CPU: a small SiLU network, trained by the optional
PyTorch tool in `optional/transport-flow`, that moves points from a uniform source rectangle
toward an image's density.

[`loadStippleTransport`](machine-learning.md#stippletransport-kt--loadstippletransport) reads the exported JSON model. [`StippleTransport.transport`](machine-learning.md#stippletransport-kt--stippletransport--transport) and
[`StippleTransport.flowMap`](machine-learning.md#stippletransport-kt--stippletransport--flowmap) integrate points through the learned velocity field (Euler or
midpoint steps), [`StippleTransport.pathsFrom`](machine-learning.md#stippletransport-kt--stippletransport--pathsfrom) returns each point's path as an [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline), and
[`StippleTransport.sourceParticles`](machine-learning.md#stippletransport-kt--stippletransport--sourceparticles) draws the source points. A temporal model also takes a movie
time, so you can draw source points once and re-transport the same list for each frame.
`StippleTransportTest` covers loading and integration.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/spatial/stippletransport.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/spatial/stippletransport/)
